title: In 1847, hand-washing cut maternity ward deaths from 18% to under 2%
body: In Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that the maternity clinic run by doctors and medical students lost about 10% of mothers to childbed fever; the midwives’ clinic lost under 4%. In 1847 his friend Jakob Kolletschka died after a scalpel nick during an autopsy. Semmelweis reasoned that **cadaverous particles** travelled from the autopsy room on doctors’ hands, and in mid-May ordered hand-washing in chlorinated lime. The death rate fell from 18.3% in April to 2.2% in June and 1.2% in July. Colleagues rejected the idea; he died in an asylum in 1865.

slides.question: In April 1847, before hand-washing began, what share of mothers in the First Clinic died?
slides.explanation: 18.3% of mothers died that April. By July, with chlorinated lime hand-washing in force, the rate was 1.2%.

slides.heading: April 1847: 18 of every 100 mothers in the doctors’ clinic died
slides.note: 18.3% that month; by July, with chlorinated-lime hand-washing in force, 1.2%

slides.alt: Bar chart of maternal deaths in Vienna’s First Clinic in 1847: 18.3% in April, then after chlorinated-lime hand-washing began in mid-May, 2.2% in June, 1.2% in July and 1.9% in August.
slides.caption: Deaths of mothers in the First Clinic in 1847, before and after hand-washing began.

left.label: Doctors’ clinic
left.text: About 10% of mothers died of childbed fever. Staff came straight from the autopsy room.

events.text: Chlorinated lime hand-washing begins; deaths plunge
Publishes his book on childbed fever; the profession stays unconvinced
Committed to an asylum by colleagues; dies 14 days later
